- Which computations need the transition and reward model?
- Which action-selection step can use a learned table directly?

**Notes:**

> This is recap
> Answers: full expected evaluation and VI/PI/Q-value-iteration backups need the transition/reward model (or its
> equivalent full outcome distribution). Greedy selection from available action values uses the Q table directly;
> extracting from state values needs one-step model lookahead. Full expectations can also be costly in large spaces.
> Target: 2 min. Sources: old DP PPTX 38–39 (summary) and 43–45 (model availability), condensed.

## 4. MT02 — Why learn from samples?

- V(s)

- V(s′)

- V(s)

- V(s′)

| Expected backup | Sample backup |
| --- | --- |
| Average over possible outcomes using the model | Use an observed transition |
| Need outcome probabilities and expected rewards | Receive (St,At,Rt+1,St+1) |

- A robot's dynamics may be unknown or unreliable.
- A simulator may produce samples even when enumerating all outcomes is impractical.
- One cheap update can still require many samples to learn accurately.
- Reinforcement Learning: Models are unknown ahead of time (Today: Sampling, Later: Model-Learning)

**Notes:**

> A simulator is a source of experience; model-free describes how the learning method uses that experience.
> For a tabular one-step update, arithmetic/value-table accesses do not scale with the number of possible
> successors; sample generation itself need not be cheap. Sampling does not by itself solve large-state-space
> representation. Ask: does observing one transition tell us that it is the only possible outcome? Answer: no.
> Sources: P4–5/P12; book §8.5 for the expected/sample distinction.
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 4–5 (backup pictures redrawn natively with V(s)/V(s′) labels; offline/online labels and future-method list removed), PPTX 12 (motivation, shortened), book §8.5.

## 5. MT03 — Side Note: Three different questions about the data

| Question | Distinction |
| --- | --- |
| Do we use or learn an environment model? | Model-based / model-free |
| Can we collect more interaction data while learning? | Online / offline (fixed data) |
| Does the behaviour generating data match the policy being evaluated? | On-policy / off-policy |

- Today: tabular, model-free, on-policy prediction of a fixed $𝜋$.

**Notes:**

> For on-policy prediction, actions in the experience follow the policy being evaluated. Off-policy prediction
> evaluates a target policy using data generated by a different behaviour policy; the target need not be
> optimal. Do not introduce correction ratios. A fixed dataset can have been collected under the target
> policy; fixed data and off-policy are not synonyms. Likewise, MC can collect episodes online and update after
> each one: waiting for termination does not make the overall learning setting offline. These distinctions
> return in Weeks 4, 11 and 12; no formal offline-RL method is taught now.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): \pi
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 13–14 (definitions replaced by this table).

## 7. MT05 — Monte Carlo: value as a mean return

- $𝑣𝜋(𝑠)=𝔼𝜋[𝐺𝑡∣𝑆𝑡=𝑠]$
- Monte Carlo prediction: follow $𝜋$, observe complete episodes, and average returns after visits to each state.
- $𝐺𝑇=0,  𝐺𝑡=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝐺𝑡+1$
- Episode: (1,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → goal; rewards −0.04, −0.04, +1; $𝛾=0.5$.
- Your turn: calculate $𝐺2$, then $𝐺1$, then $𝐺0$ for our episode.

- $𝐺2=1,  𝐺1=−0.04+0.5(1)=0.46,  𝐺0=−0.04+0.5(0.46)=0.19$
- One observed return is a sample, not the expectation.

**Notes:**

> About 1 minute rationale, 2 minutes student calculation, 2 minutes discussion. Click: answers. T = 3 here; the
> terminal entry reward is in G_2, not in G_3. The unknown quantity is the expected return; an episode supplies
> an observed target. This complete-return MC method needs the relevant episode to terminate. A truncated
> partial sum is not the same target. The book writes v_π; course notation is v^π.
> Sources: book §5.1; Silver pp. 4–7; CS234 pp. 10–14.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): v^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t\mid S_t=s] | \pi | G_T=0,\qquad G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1} | \gamma=0.5 | G_2 | G_1 | G_0 | G_2=1,\qquad G_1=-0.04+0.5(1)=0.46,\qquad G_0=-0.04+0.5(0.46)=0.19
>
> Target: 5 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 16–17 (value/return equations, converted), book §5.1, Silver lecture 4 pp. 4–7, CS234 lecture 3 pp. 10–14.

## 8. MT06 — Which visits count?

- Episode: (1,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → goal

- First-visit MC: include only the first visit to a state in each episode.
- Every-visit MC: include every visit to that state.
- Question: what sample mean does each produce after this one episode? (For (1,1))

| Visit to (1,1) | Return following that visit |
| --- | --- |
| First, t=0 | 0.19 |
| Second, t=1 | 0.46 |

- Answer: first-visit $0.19$; every-visit $(0.19+0.46)/2=0.325$.

**Notes:**

> Ask students which returns belong in each average before revealing it (click: answer). At (1,2), either
> convention includes the single return 1. N(s) counts included returns: first visits for first-visit MC, all
> visits for every-visit MC. Returns from repeated visits within an episode are correlated; do not call them
> independent episodes or assert that every finite-sample MC estimate is unbiased. Under the usual
> fixed-policy/visitation assumptions both visit conventions are consistent. These numbers are sample means;
> later we explicitly switch to constant-step updates. Sources: book §5.1, CS234 p. 26.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): 0.19 | (0.19+0.46)/2=0.325
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 18 (repeated-state question) and 21 (first/every-visit distinction), book §5.1, CS234 lecture 3 p. 26.

## 9. MT07 — From an average to an incremental update

| Step size for MC | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 1/N(s)* | Exact sample mean of included returns |
| Constant α | Recency weighting; initialization can still matter, better for non-stationary problems |

- *This is a special case of decayed α that meets the Robbins–Monro conditions for convergence, but not all decay schedules work

- For one newly included return $𝐺𝑡$, first increment $𝑁(𝑠)$:
- $𝑁(𝑠)←𝑁(𝑠)+1$
- $𝑉(𝑠)←(𝑁(𝑠)−1)𝑉(𝑠)+𝐺𝑡𝑁(𝑠)=𝑉(𝑠)+1𝑁(𝑠)[𝐺𝑡−𝑉(𝑠)]$
- A common update form
- $𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+𝛼[𝑈𝑡−𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$
- $𝑈𝑡$: target. $𝛼$: fraction of the discrepancy used for this update.

**Notes:**

> The right-hand V(s) is its old value; after incrementing the count, N(s)−1 returns contributed to that old
> mean. Show the algebra, not just the final rule. Constant α weights recent targets more and can be useful
> when the policy changes later; here π is fixed. For this presentation take 0 < α ≤ 1. A first-visit sample
> mean and a constant-step estimate are different estimators even when fed the same return. No gradient aside
> or convergence-sum derivation. Sources: P18–20; book §§2.4–2.5; Silver p. 11.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): G_t | N(s) | N(s)\leftarrow N(s)+1 | V(s)\leftarrow\frac{(N(s)-1)V(s)+G_t}{N(s)}=V(s)+\frac{1}{N(s)}[G_t-V(s)] | V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha[U_t-V(S_t)] | U_t | \alpha
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 18–20 (running-mean equations; V̄ → V, visit indices removed, N(s) kept, old δ for the MC error not used), book §§2.4–2.5, Silver lecture 4 p. 11.

## 10. MT07a — First-visit MC prediction

- 1. Fix $𝜋$. Initialize $𝑉(𝑠)=0$ and $𝑁(𝑠)=0$ for nonterminal states.
- 2. Generate a complete episode following $𝜋$.
- 3. Compute its returns backwards: $𝐺𝑇=0$, then $𝐺𝑡=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝐺𝑡+1$.
- 4. Scan the episode in time order. At the first visit to each state:
- increment $𝑁(𝑆𝑡)$;
- update $𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+1𝑁(𝑆𝑡)[𝐺𝑡−𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$.
- 5. Repeat with another episode.

- For constant-step MC, replace $1/𝑁(𝑆𝑡)$ by $𝛼$ in step 4. The first-visit rule stays.
- Question: How do the steps change if we do the every-visit version?

**Notes:**

> "First" means earliest in the episode, not first encountered in the backward return calculation. Students
> need to understand this order before implementing an update kernel. No list of returns need be retained
> across episodes; the current episode still needs enough information to compute its returns. For every-visit
> MC omit the first-visit restriction. Spoken caveat: fixed-policy tabular convergence requires sufficient
> visits and suitable step sizes; constant α generally leaves fluctuations in noisy problems. The Robbins–Monro
> step-size conditions are one source of such guarantees, not a proof that every constant-step process must
> fluctuate. We will compare mechanisms today, not prove convergence.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): \pi | V(s)=0 | N(s)=0 | G_T=0 | G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1} | N(S_t) | V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\frac{1}{N(S_t)}[G_t-V(S_t)] | 1/N(S_t) | \alpha
>
> Target: 2 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 21 (algorithm picture; rebuilt as editable text without its Returns lists), book §5.1.

## 12. MT09 — A sampled Bellman target – Temporal Difference (TD) Learning

- 1. Recall the Bellman expectation equation:
- $𝑣𝜋(𝑠)=𝔼𝜋[𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑣𝜋(𝑆𝑡+1)∣𝑆𝑡=𝑠]$

- 2. Use one observed transition and the current next-state estimate:
- $𝑈𝑡=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑉(𝑆𝑡+1)$

- 3. Compare the target with the current estimate, then update:
- $𝛿𝑡=𝑈𝑡−𝑉(𝑆𝑡),  𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+𝛼𝛿𝑡$

- Bootstrapping: use an existing value estimate in a new update target.
- The expected TD target is a Bellman backup of the current $𝑉$; it need not equal $𝑣𝜋$.

**Notes:**

> Reveal in order (two clicks: step 2; then step 3 with the bootstrapping line). The two approximations are
> sampling the expectation and replacing the unknown true successor value with V. For a fixed table under π,
> averaging this target gives the DP evaluation backup of that table. Correct successor values are sufficient,
> not necessary, for that expectation to equal the true value at a given state: successor errors may cancel.
> Do not use "unbiased only if the whole table is exact." A single target is not guaranteed closer to truth.
> This is one-step TD, called TD(0); the zero is part of the method's name, not α = 0. At a terminal successor
> V = 0, so the target is just the observed entry reward. No maximization: this is fixed-policy prediction.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): v^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R_{t+1}+\gamma v^{\pi}(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s] | U_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1}) | \delta_t=U_t-V(S_t),\qquad V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha\delta_t | V | v^{\pi}
>
> Target: 2.5 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 24 (bootstrapping explanation) and 25–26 (TD equations; reward index, barred values and policy marks converted), book §6.1 printed 119–121 / PDF 141–143.

## 13. MT09a — TD(0) prediction

- Update after observing the transition. Read the current table before changing it.

- Fix $𝜋$ and choose $𝛼$. Initialize the nonterminal estimates; set $𝑉(terminal)=0$.
- At each transition:
- 1. Take $𝐴𝑡$ according to $𝜋$; observe $𝑅𝑡+1$ and $𝑆𝑡+1$.
- 2. Form $𝑈𝑡=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑉(𝑆𝑡+1)$.
- 3. Update $𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+𝛼[𝑈𝑡−𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$.
- 4. Advance to the next state; if terminal, end the episode.

**Notes:**

> This matters for self-transitions: calculate the target before overwriting the same table entry. Keep the
> terminal value at zero. In a continuing discounted task, continue taking transitions without an episode-end
> test. This does not make the displayed TD rule an average-reward algorithm; the objective contrast later
> changes the question, not this algorithm. The fixed-policy, tabular, adequate-visitation and
> suitable-step-size qualifications apply to convergence. No theorem or function-approximation guarantee is
> added here.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): \pi | \alpha | V(\text{terminal})=0 | A_t | R_{t+1} | S_{t+1} | U_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1}) | V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha[U_t-V(S_t)]
>
> Target: 1.5 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 27 (algorithm picture; rebuilt as editable text), book §6.1.

## 15. MT10 — Your turn: MC and TD on the same episode

| Method / event | Target Ut | Estimate being changed | Value after update |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MC, first (1,1) visit | ? | ? | ? |
| MC, first (1,2) visit | ? | ? | ? |
| TD, t=0 | ? | ? | ? |
| TD, t=1 | ? | ? | ? |
| TD, t=2 | ? | ? | ? |

| Method / event | Target Ut | Estimate being changed | Value after update |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MC, first (1,1) visit | 0.19 | V((1,1)) | 0.095 |
| MC, first (1,2) visit | 1 | V((1,2)) | 0.5 |
| TD, t=0 | −0.04 | V((1,1)) | −0.02 |
| TD, t=1 | −0.04 | V((1,1)) | −0.03 |
| TD, t=2 | 1 | V((1,2)) | 0.5 |

- MC and TD have different targets and update schedules; this is not a performance ranking.

- (1,1) → (1,1) → (1,2) → goal;   rewards −0.04, −0.04, +1;   returns 0.19, 0.46, 1
- Reset each method independently: $𝑉=0$, $𝛾=0.5$, constant $𝛼=0.5$.
- 1. First-visit MC: update each state's first visit using its completed return.
- 2. TD(0): update after each transition, in time order.
- 3. Why does the goal reward affect the estimates differently?

**Notes:**

> PROTECTED student reasoning. Allow roughly 1 minute instructions/reset, 4 minutes students calculate,
> 3 minutes answer discussion, 1 minute interpretation. Click: answer table.
> Constant-step first-visit MC: 0 + 0.5(0.19 − 0) = 0.095; skip the second (1,1) visit; 0 + 0.5(1 − 0) = 0.5
> at (1,2). These differ from MT06's sample means because α is now fixed at 0.5.
> TD t=0: target −0.04 + 0.5(0) = −0.04, error −0.04, new V((1,1)) = −0.02.
> TD t=1: V((1,2)) is still zero, so target −0.04; error −0.04 − (−0.02) = −0.02; new
> V((1,1)) = −0.02 + 0.5(−0.02) = −0.03.
> TD t=2: target 1 + 0.5(0) = 1; error 1; new V((1,2)) = 0.5. No update to the terminal state. (2,1) stays
> zero in both tables because it is unvisited.
> MC uses the realized goal reward immediately in the earlier completed-return target. Online TD's earlier
> updates happened before the successor estimate learned from the goal. Later visits can propagate this
> information; there is no extra backward TD sweep at the end of this pass.
> Equal α does not isolate only target choice: first-visit MC updates (1,1) once; TD updates it twice. Do not
> interpret a negative estimate after one episode as proof of failure or positive estimates as proof of
> optimism.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): V=0 | \gamma=0.5 | \alpha=0.5
>
> Target: 9 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 21/27 (algorithm structures), MT04 trajectory, new answer table; numbers checked by scripts/check_mc_td_claude.py section 3.

## 17. MT12 — Sampling and bootstrapping

- DP: all successors, one step

- terminal

- MC: one path to termination

- TD(0): one sampled step

| Method | Uses sampled experience? | Bootstraps from value estimates? | What supplies the target? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DP expected evaluation backup | No | Yes | Model-weighted reward and successor values |
| Complete-return MC | Yes | No | Observed return through termination |
| TD(0) | Yes | Yes | One observed reward and next-state estimate |

- Sampling: use observed outcomes in place of a full expectation.   Bootstrapping: use a value estimate in the target.
- Check: Which needs a model? Which must wait for the completed return? Which can update before the episode ends?

**Notes:**

> Answers: the displayed DP backup; complete-return MC; TD(0). Samples can come from real interaction or a
> simulator. For a fixed table, one sample TD target averages to a DP evaluation backup; the current table
> itself may be inaccurate. No claim that each sampled update reduces error. The classification concerns these
> three specific methods, not every possible algorithm called DP or MC. Detailed bias/variance, batch learning
> and n-step targets belong in 3.2. Do not add the old full unified-method diagram, λ axis or eligibility
> traces. Open circles are states, solid dots are actions.
>
> Target: 4 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 37–39 (Silver backup pictures; redrawn natively because "T" labels are embedded; non-Markov claims removed) and 40 (classification), Silver lecture 4 pp. 26–29.

> busy. Discounted return is already one meaningful objective for such a task. We now contrast it with average
> reward. All rewards are received on the stated transitions and each transition consumes one equal unit of
> time. Students identify the two reward sequences before the next slide. No policy learning algorithm is

## 19. MT13a — Discounted return and average reward

| Policy | Average reward per step | Discounted return from ready, γ=0.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steady service | ? | ? |
| Large jobs | ? | ? |

| Policy | Average reward per step | Discounted return from ready, γ=0.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steady service | 0.8 | 1.6 |
| Large jobs | (0 + 2)/2 = 1 | 4/3 ≈ 1.333 |

- The objective changes the ranking: discounted return prefers steady service; average reward prefers large jobs.
- Self-Study Suggestion: Sutton & Barto §10.3 for the differential return and values that average-reward methods learn.

- Average reward: expected reward per step over a long run
- For the policies in this service example, starting from ready:
- $𝑟(𝜋)≐lim𝑡→∞1𝑡𝔼𝜋[𝑅1+𝑅2+⋯+𝑅𝑡∣𝑆0=ready]$

**Notes:**

> About 1 minute students compute rates, 1 minute discounted comparison, 1 minute interpretation. Ask for the
> average-reward entries first; click: full table; click: ranking line. Show the rates as the proportion of
> total reward to elapsed steps. Discounted values:
> Steady: 0.8 + 0.5×0.8 + … = 0.8/(1−0.5) = 1.6.
> Large jobs: 0 + 0.5×2 + 0.5³×2 + … = 1/(1−0.5²) = 4/3.
> The job pays more per step in the long run but delays its first payment. This is an objective choice;
> neither objective is universally correct.
> The alternating policy is periodic. Its time average exists, but its individual expected rewards oscillate;
> do not write r(π) = lim 𝔼[R_t] or claim convergence to a stationary distribution. No ergodicity lesson is
> required. The displayed definition is scoped to this example, avoiding a claim that every MDP has a
> start-independent average reward.
> The discounted TD(0) rule taught earlier does not by itself learn this average-reward objective. No
> differential returns, differential Bellman equations, average-reward algorithm or approximation teaser here.
> MT13 and MT13a together keep exactly the accepted five-minute contrast.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): r(\pi)\doteq\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R_1+R_2+\cdots+R_t\mid S_0=\text{ready}]
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Value Function Approximation PPTX 37 (average-reward definition, restricted to the time-average form), book §10.3 Eq. 10.6 printed 249 / PDF 271 (Eq. 10.7 not used).

## 22. MT16 — Bias and variance describe repeated samples

- At the same state, repeat the sampling experiment while holding the current table fixed.
- Bias: mean target minus the true value.
- Variance: spread of targets around their own mean.
- Mean squared error = variance + bias².

| Equally likely targets | Mean | Bias | Variance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.0 or 2.0 | 1.0 | ? | ? |
| 0.8 or 1.0 | 0.9 | ? | ? |

| Equally likely targets | Mean | Bias | Variance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.0 or 2.0 | 1.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 |
| 0.8 or 1.0 | 0.9 | −0.1 | 0.01 |

- Illustration, true value 1.0:

**Notes:**

> These are illustrative target distributions, not experiment results or labels for MC/TD. Ask which pair is
> less spread out, then reveal the last two columns (click: answers). Zero bias alone need not mean lower
> squared error: here the MSEs are 1 and 0.02. One observed target cannot establish its mean or spread.
> Distinguish a random update target from the estimate after a history of updates. Keep this to meaning and the
> simple numerical illustration; no statistical derivation live.
>
> Target: 2 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 30 (framing; unconditional statements replaced), CS234 lecture 3 pp. 23–24.

|  | MC | TD(0) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target | Gt | Rt+1+γV(St+1) |
| Samples | Remaining episode | One transition |
| Uses the current value table in the target? | No | Yes |

- Question: On the grid, which random transitions affect each target for the start state?

- $𝔼𝜋[𝐺𝑡∣𝑆𝑡=𝑠]=𝑣𝜋(𝑠)$
- $𝔼𝜋[𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑉(𝑆𝑡+1)∣𝑆𝑡=𝑠]-𝑣𝜋(𝑠)=𝛾 𝔼𝜋[𝑉(𝑆𝑡+1)-𝑣𝜋(𝑆𝑡+1)∣𝑆𝑡=𝑠]$
- MC has an unbiased target. TD's target can inherit error from the table.

**Notes:**

> About 1 minute on the table, 1 on the expectation equation, 1 on the grid question. MC includes every later
> slip and reward; TD(0) includes the next transition and the fixed table. Random actions also enter in
> problems with a stochastic policy; the grid policy is deterministic. The TD expression is a Bellman
> expectation backup, not necessarily the true value. Correct successor values are sufficient for zero target
> bias, not necessary: successor errors can cancel. MC does not use V in its target, but a constant-α MC
> estimate can still depend on its initialization. In noisy problems constant α generally leaves estimates
> fluctuating.
> Say: "Bootstrapping often reduces sampling variability, but a poor table can reverse that comparison." No
> universal variance ordering for arbitrary learned tables.
> Optional explanation if asked: with fixed correct V in a Markov task under a fixed policy, and finite second
> moments, the TD target is the conditional expectation of the return given the first observed transition;
> total variance gives its variance no greater than the return's. Longer true-value targets condition on
> longer prefixes. This argument does not cover arbitrary inaccurate V. Counterexample: zero rewards throughout
> and equally likely nonterminal successors with V = +1/−1 yield a variable TD target but a constant zero
> return. Do not add a proof or counterexample slide.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t\mid S_t=s]=v^{\pi}(s) | \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s]-v^{\pi}(s)=\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[V(S_{t+1})-v^{\pi}(S_{t+1})\mid S_t=s]

> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 30 (equations rewritten), book §6.2, CS234 lecture 3 pp. 24–26.

## 26. MT18 — Learning repeatedly from a fixed batch

- Question: Can repeated learning from the same data lead to different answers?

- We have a fixed set of complete episodes. No new experience arrives.
- For each pass through the batch:
- 1. Hold V fixed while computing each visit's increment.
- 2. Add the increments for each state.
- 3. Apply those sums, then start the next pass.
- $increment=𝛼[𝑈𝑡-𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$
- MC uses the observed return. TD uses the reward and the next state's estimate.

**Notes:**

> Set up the experiment before the puzzle. "Fixed V" lasts for one pass, not all passes; bootstrapped targets
> change on later passes. This is the batch convention of book §6.3, not online updates applied immediately on
> each visit, and not a first introduction to modern offline-control problems. Use sufficiently small α for
> stable batch iteration. In this small tabular example each method approaches its own fixed point. Repeating a
> batch changes computation, not the amount of collected experience. The next example asks about the converged
> batch answers, not one pass from zero.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): \text{increment}=\alpha[U_t-V(S_t)]
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 33 (finite-data question; batch curve omitted), book §6.3 printed p. 126 / PDF 148, Sutton TD slides pp. 21–31.

## 28. MT19a — Two batch answers from the same data

*Image `native:pic:34:Picture 4`*

- Empirical model from the eight episodes

- MC: fit the observed returns at each state.
- TD: use the observed transitions and share the continuation estimate at B.

|  | Batch MC | Batch TD(0) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B | V(B)=6/8=0.75 | V(B)=6/8=0.75 |
| A | Its only observed return was 0 | Its observed successor was B, with reward 0 |
| Answer at A | V(A)=0 | V(A)=0+V(B)=0.75 |

- Data: A →(0) B →(0) terminal ×1;  B →(1) terminal ×6;  B →(0) terminal ×1.

- Question: When is it reasonable to reuse all the B outcomes after arriving from A?

- Model picture: old course slides (book Example 6.4). Both terminal branches have continuation zero.

**Notes:**

> About 1 minute for B, 1 for the MC answer, 2 for the TD/model explanation, 1 for the question. Reusing B's
> outcomes assumes the future from B does not depend on arriving via A versus starting in B: the Markov
> property. Batch MC minimizes squared error on observed returns. It fits A's one return exactly, but that does
> not establish best future prediction. At B the observed targets include both 0 and 1, so neither method fits
> every return exactly. Batch TD's fixed point equals the value of the maximum-likelihood empirical Markov
> model in this example, often called the certainty-equivalence answer. TD itself need not build or solve that
> model.
> The data do not prove this empirical model is the true environment. With only one A visit, both answers
> reflect limited evidence. If the label B hides relevant history, pooling all its continuations can mislead.
> MC avoids bootstrapping through that aliased state but does not repair partial observability. Do not present
> this as proof TD always wins or merely as a bias–variance illustration: the central distinction is return
> fitting versus Markov structure in batch learning. Ordinary online updates need not reach either batch answer
> after one pass.
>
> Target: 5 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 34 (empirical Markov diagram) and 35 (two solution interpretations, corrected), book §6.3 pp. 127–128 / PDF 149–150, Silver lecture 4, Sutton TD slides pp. 21–31.

## 30. MT21 — The n-step target

- Before termination, replace the unobserved tail by the current estimate:
- $𝐺𝑡:𝑡+1=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑉(𝑆𝑡+1)$
- $𝐺𝑡:𝑡+2=𝑅𝑡+1+𝛾𝑅𝑡+2+𝛾2𝑉(𝑆𝑡+2)$

- For a positive integer n and a visit $𝑡<𝑇$:
- If $𝑡+𝑛<𝑇$:
- $𝐺𝑡:𝑡+𝑛=𝑖=1𝑛𝛾𝑖-1𝑅𝑡+𝑖+𝛾𝑛𝑉(𝑆𝑡+𝑛)$
- If $𝑡+𝑛≥𝑇$:
- $𝐺𝑡:𝑡+𝑛=𝑖=1𝑇-𝑡𝛾𝑖-1𝑅𝑡+𝑖=𝐺𝑡$

- Same update form when the target becomes available:
- $𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+𝛼[𝐺𝑡:𝑡+𝑛-𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$

**Notes:**

> One minute expanding the first two targets, two for deriving the general/terminal cases (click: general
> case), one for the update (click: update). Split the complete return into n observed rewards and its
> remaining discounted tail; replace that tail by V. The last observed reward has weight γ^(n−1), and the
> continuation has weight γ^n. At or past termination there is no continuation, no fictitious extra reward and
> no state lookup beyond T. The terminal-entry payoff is already included once. V means the table available
> when computing the delayed update, immediately before that update, unless a frozen snapshot is explicitly
> requested. Thus these equations do not silently mean the old table from the original visit time t. Use the
> in-place form to avoid a new update-clock symbol.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): G_{t:t+1}=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1}) | G_{t:t+2}=R_{t+1}+\gamma R_{t+2}+\gamma^{2}V(S_{t+2}) | t<T | t+n<T | G_{t:t+n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\gamma^{i-1}R_{t+i}+\gamma^{n}V(S_{t+n}) | t+n\geq T | G_{t:t+n}=\sum_{i=1}^{T-t}\gamma^{i-1}R_{t+i}=G_t | V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha[G_{t:t+n}-V(S_t)]
>
> Target: 4 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 43 (equations converted to the guide notation; reward indices fixed), book §7.1 eqs. 7.1–7.2 printed pp. 143–144 / PDF 165–166.

## 31. MT21a — When can the update happen?

- For the visit at time t, wait until n further transitions or termination, whichever comes first.

| Experience observed | Earliest eligible work |
| --- | --- |
| One transition | Wait, unless it terminated |
| Two transitions | Update the visit at time 0 |
| Later transitions | Update visits as their targets become available |
| Episode terminates | Complete all remaining visits in their original order |

- For n = 2:

- Terminal completion needs no further environment transitions.
- $𝑉(𝑆𝑡)←𝑉(𝑆𝑡)+𝛼[𝐺𝑡:𝑡+𝑛-𝑉(𝑆𝑡)]$

**Notes:**

> Distinguish environment interaction from processing pending updates. Before n rewards arrive, the target
> usually needs data we have not seen. If the episode ends sooner, the complete return is already known. Finish
> pending visits before starting the next episode. A repeated state may receive multiple updates. A target equal
> to the complete return does not by itself make the update schedule first-visit MC; n-step prediction updates
> each visit. The next exercise shows the terminal flush explicitly.
>
> Equation sources (LaTeX): V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha[G_{t:t+n}-V(S_t)]
>
> Target: 2 min. Sources: book §7.1 algorithm p. 144 / PDF 166 (without its auxiliary τ notation).

| Start | C | Middle state |
| Moves | Left/right with probability 0.5 | Same |
| Terminal-entry rewards | Left 0, right +1 | Left −1, right +1 |
| Other rewards / γ | 0 / 1 | 0 / 1 |
| Initial nonterminal V | 0.5 | 0 |

- Book Example 7.1 (Sutton & Barto, 2018, p. 145).

**Notes:**

> This is the book's distinct experiment in Example 7.1, not a new run of the grid and not a continuation of
> the five-state training curve. The same sampled walks are reused across all parameter settings. The true
> values are −0.9, −0.8, …, 0.9, including 0 at the middle; give this if asked, no second derivation. Average
> the per-episode RMS errors; do not take one square root after pooling all runs/episodes. Announce the metric
> because the next graph's horizontal axis is α, not episodes.
>
> Target: 2 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 44 (experiment framing, expanded with the changed conventions), book Example 7.1 and Figure 7.2 p. 145 / PDF 167.

## 36. MT23a — n and step size interact

*Image `native:pic:44:Picture 5`*

- Each curve fixes n. Horizontal axis: α. Lower error is better.
- Question: Is the best n the same at every α? What can we conclude from the low points of these curves?

- Intermediate n performs best in this experiment. Step size matters too.
- The target uses the table only if the episode is still running after n steps. A longer horizon reaches a complete return more often, but can also add sampling variability and delay.

- Plot: Sutton & Barto (2018), Figure 7.2 (19-state random walk).

**Notes:**

> Two minutes to read axes/curves, two for discussion and the mechanism (click: conclusion and mechanism). The
> plot reports early learning over ten episodes, not asymptotic performance. For this undiscounted walk γ^n = 1:
> discounting does not reduce the bootstrap weight. The chance that the target reaches termination instead of
> the table changes with n. With an imperfect table, more sampled rewards often increase variability but there
> is no universal ordering. A shrinking bias bound does not prove monotonic bias reduction or that some
> intermediate n must win. Large finite n curves such as 256/512 are not literally MC on every possible episode.
> This plot motivates a sensitivity check, not a universal n recommendation.
> Optional, notes only: for a fixed table and starting state s, the absolute error of the expected n-step target
> is bounded by γ^n × probability the episode is still running after those n transitions × the largest absolute
> error in V. The probability is conditional on the starting state and policy. Terminal errors are zero. For
> γ = 1 only the survival factor changes this bound. This is a statement about the expected target with a fixed
> table, not each noisy sample or the evolving online learning curve.
>
> Target: 4 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 44 (Figure 7.2; old best-of-all-n bridge to λ removed), book §7.1 eq. 7.3 and Example 7.1.

> would win" nor "no wider search could change anything" follows from the displayed settings. Each method may

**Notes:**

> One minute vote and variable episode lengths (click: budget table), one minute batch/compute (click:
> question), one minute consolidation. Episode lengths vary. Our two independently seeded methods need not see
> equal transition totals at the same episode count, even though they use the same start and transition
> distribution. Under the generated every-visit protocol both methods make one update per visited nonterminal
> state, but their timing, storage and total sampled transitions can differ. MC waits for episode completion; TD
> updates online. Repeating the same batch adds data-processing cost without new interactions. For stronger
> interaction-matched claims, compare at matched cumulative transitions; wall-clock claims need measurements.

## 41. MT25 — Choosing between MC, TD and n-step targets

| Question | MC | TD(0) | n-step TD |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Target | Complete return | One reward + V | n rewards + V if still running |
| Earliest update | Episode end | Next transition | n transitions or episode end |
| Target error | Unbiased under the fixed policy | Can inherit table bias | Horizon changes reliance on the table |
| Sampling variability | Often high | Often lower with a useful table | Often grows with horizon; not guaranteed |
| Useful when | Complete episodes are available; avoid a bootstrap target | Need immediate updates or discounted continuing prediction | Can wait for more evidence before bootstrapping |
| Dependence on V in the target | None | Direct | Through a surviving continuation |

- TD shares continuation estimates using the Markov assumption. MC's completed target avoids that bootstrap; it does not solve partial observability.
- Choice needs evidence: compare runs, tuning and budgets on the task.
- Next: control with sampled targets. λ mixtures: Week 8.

**Notes:**

> About two minutes to revisit the practical choices and one to connect forward. This is the reference slide the
> instructor asked to keep (deck decision D14). The variability row states common tendencies, not a theorem for
> arbitrary V. For n reaching the episode end, the target is the full return; every-visit versus first-visit
> scheduling can still differ. MC's target has no V, but finite-data/constant-α estimates can retain
> initialization effects. TD/n-step targets can inherit errors from initial tables. For continuing tasks, the
> methods discussed here are ordinary discounted prediction; do not imply the same formula solves average-reward
> differential prediction. The earlier five-minute objective contrast introduced no such algorithm. No
> function-approximation convergence promises, universal MC/TD ranking or new λ derivation.
>
> Target: 3 min. Sources: old Model-Free Prediction PPTX 29/31/36 (reference-table purpose; claims qualified under review R28–R29), book §§6.2–6.3 and §7.1.
